 The second half of the 2026 college football season has arrived for the Aggies, who must win four of their final six games to achieve bowl eligibility.
 Utah State has yet to prevail on the road this season and the next challenge will be an explosive Texas State offense — one that shattered the program record with 716 yards of total offense in a 66-27 drubbing of visiting Colorado State last Thursday. 
 The Bobcats will welcome the Aggies to UFCU Stadium for a Saturday evening Homecoming showdown. The opening kickoff in this Pac-12 game is scheduled for 5:30 p.m. and it will be televised on the CBS Sports Network.
 “The bye week came at a critical time,” said USU head coach Bronco Mendenhall, whose team was able to recuperate following a come-from-behind 17-16 win over visiting Washington State on Oct. 9. “We were having to start to alter practice prior to the Washington State game and the game prior to that. But having won two of our last three (games) there’s a toll that just that type of physical practice takes to prepare a team to keep pushing it forward besides the games. And that is happening with us, as well as teams around the country. We anticipate three, maybe four players back for this week, which will be great and at positions of need.”
 The Pac-12’s weekly injury report was released Thursday, and three potential starters could be back for the Aggies (2-4, 1-1). Jackson Nelson hasn’t played since grading out well as the starting right tackle in USU’s season-opener against Idaho State. He is listed as “probable” to play against Texas State (3-3, 1-1). Two other USU starters who missed the WSU game with an injury are listed as “questionable” for Saturday’s contest in linebacker James Jennette and safety Chapman Lewis.
 Eli Wood, one of the most productive receivers in the Pac-12 and was recently added to the Biletnikoff Award Watch List, is also listed as “questionable” for the Aggies, as are three other key cogs in slot target Javon Robinson, offensive lineman John Randle Jr. and linebacker Jordan Pendleton.
 Potentially having the lion’s share of their top defensive players will be crucial for the Aggies against an opponent that ranks first in the Pac-12 in total offense (562.3 yards per game), rushing offense (303.5 ypg) and third-down conversion percentage (54.8). The Bobcats are second in the conference in scoring offense (40.2 points an outing), to boot.
 The Aggies have been rock solid on defense this season as they rank first in the Pac-12 in passing efficiency allowed (118.9), second in total defense (359.7 ypg) and fourth in rushing defense (140.8 ypg). 
 “An up-tempo team,” Mendenhall said of TSU. “They play really fast. They score a lot of points. Super aggressive. Really well coached and, yeah, I’m looking forward to the matchup.”
 The Pac-12 has the top two running backs at the FBS level in terms of yards per game in Texas State’s Torrance Burgess and Boise State’s Dylan Riley. Burgess is barely ahead of Riley as he now averages 139.7 ypg, thanks to his massive performance last Thursday against the reeling Rams.
 Burgess, who was injured last season and was limited to four games, accounted for 224 yards and four touchdowns on 24 carries against CSU. The former UTEP starter also added 52 yards on three receptions on his way to being selected as the Pac-12 Offensive Player of the Week.
 The Bobcats went off for 503 rushing yards against the Rams, which is the most by any FBS program since 2021 and TSU’s most since transitioning from the FCS to FBS level in 2012. 
 “Yeah, really dynamic and physical,” Mendenhall said of the 5-foot-8, 176-pound Burgess. “Very difficult to tackle. Rarely does one player get him on the ground. You better wrap up, as he breaks tackles and he’s dynamic, so he’s runs for efficiency, but he also runs explosively. Besides the chains moving, he can also kind of break it for the distance. Gosh, 500-something yards of rushing offense against Colorado State, that’s a lot of rush yards, so even though this team is up-tempo … make no mistakes, this is a running football team and one that’s physical. … They’ve done a really good job recruiting at the running back position.”
 Two other Bobcats have been very productive toting the pigskin this season in standout quarterback Brad Jackson and tailback Davian Jackson, a former Mississippi State player. Brad has chipped in with 367 yards and four TDs, and Davian with 315 yards and five scores. Brad is listed as “questionable” for Saturday’s game.
 Brad Jackson is a proven commodity as a signal caller, one who threw for 3,224 yards and 21 TDs, plus rushed for 744 yards and an impressive 17 scores, on his way to garnering third-team all-Sun Belt Conference honors a year ago. He completed a whopping 71.3 percent of his passes last season and has completed 67.5 percent of them, plus ranks second in the league with 239.5 ypg, in ’26. Jackson has been intercepted five times this season, but has also tossed 14 TDs.
 “I think the quarterback’s exceptional,” Mendenhall said. “I think he throws it well and I think he runs it well. I think he makes great decisions. I think he manages their offense at a really high level. I would liken him experience wise to Boise State’s quarterback, right? That doesn’t mean similar in style, but the way he runs their offense precise and detailed and makes great decisions. … An experienced and effective quarterback changes each team and, yeah, they have a good one.”
 The Bobcats brought back their potent one-two receiving punch this season in all-Sun Belt performers Chris Dawn Jr. and Beau Sparks. Sparks finished with 1,200 yards and 10 TDs a year ago, while Dawn added 1,007 yards. Texas State is running the ball a lot more this season, but Dawn still has 348 yards and four TDs on 29 catches, followed by Sparks with 301 yards on 19. 
 Texas State welcomed back seven offensive starters from last year’s 7-6 team that blew out Rice in the Armed Forces Bowl. 
 The Bobcats, who brought back four defensive starters, have been pretty shaky on that side of ball as they have allowed 32.2 points, 297.3 yards passing and 424.3 total yards an outing. TSU, additionally, only has five takeaways — four interceptions and one fumble recovery — in six games. Mendenhall, however, feels some of those statistics are a bit skewed.
 “Sound, physical, fast,” Mendenhall said of TSU’s defense. “They’re playing with a lead, their defense is a playing with a lead most of the time, so (opposing) teams are trying to catch up and keep up with their offense. So, many teams are having to throw it maybe disproportionately to try to close the gap. (But) I think they’re coached really well and, yeah, I think they’re playing confidently and I think they’re a football team as the season goes you can see them just continuing to build momentum and on both sides.”
 Strong safety Jayden Bradley leads the team in tackles with 44, followed by linebackers Terrence Cooks II and Ayden Jones with 34 apiece and cornerback Craig Royal Jr. with 31. Cooks is the team leader in tackles for loss with 4.0, while 6-5 defensive end Tyreme Jackson has 2.5 sacks and one forced fumble to his credit this season and cornerback Trez Moore has broken up six passes, which is tied for the top spot in the conference. 
 Cooks, a former TCU and Texas player, contributed with 50 tackles, including 5.5 for a loss, for the Bobcats a year ago, while Jones added 54 tackles and 6.5 TFLs. Moore, a former UTEP player, is one of four guys on the team with one INT this season.
 The Bobcats have had their struggles getting after opposing quarterbacks as they only have delivered 5.0 sacks in six games, but they have only allowed 6.0, to their credit.
 Texas State has an explosive weapon on special teams in Dameon Crowe, who returned a punt 77 yards to the house last month against Incarnate Word and has averaged 22.7 yards on six punt returns, which ranks first in the conference.
 The Bobcats are 3-1 at home this season, with wins over North Texas (49-35), Incarnate Word (61-10) and CSU (66-27). Their lone setback was a 31-26 nail-biter against a now 6-1 UTSA squad.
 “Yeah, it looks like they belong, it looks like they fit right in and it looks like they’re a great addition to the league,” Mendenhall said. “… I think Texas State is a really good team.”
 NOTES 
 * The two programs have only played once before, with USU prevailing 38-7 when both teams were in the WAC in 2012. The Aggies won the conference title and 11 games that season, which was Texas State’s first as a FBS program. 
 * Texas State head coach GJ Kinne was the starting QB for Tulsa in its 24-21 loss to Mendenhall-coached BYU in the 2011 Armed Forces Bowl. Kinne completed 17 of 31 passes for 214 yards, three TDs and zero INTs in that contest. Kinne is in his fourth season as TSU’s head coach and has a record of 26-19. 
 “(Kinne) was a very good player and also he’s leading a a really good program,” Mendenhall said while reminiscing about that bowl game.
